title: Occasion, date and setting
short: Probably drafted in 1851, when Arnold married and visited Dover; not published until New Poems (1867).
body: Most editors date the poem to 1851, the year Arnold married Frances Lucy Wightman; the couple stayed at Dover that June and passed through again in the autumn on the way to the Continent. A pencil draft of the first 28 lines survives on the back of a sheet of notes on Empedocles, which Tinker and Lowry described; it ends with a shorthand reference to the closing 'Ah love' passage, so the rest of the poem seems already to have existed. Earlier datings (1849-50) have been proposed, but they rest on the Empedocles notes rather than on any record of a visit to Dover. Arnold held the poem back for sixteen years, printing it only in New Poems (1867), so a lyric of 1851 reached readers after Darwin's Origin (1859) and the Essays and Reviews controversy (1860), which coloured how it was read. The opening sentence is flatly declarative and calm; everything that follows unsettles it.

anchor: on the French coast the light
title: the French coast
short: Across the Strait of Dover, about twenty miles wide, a lighthouse on the French shore near Calais flashes and vanishes.
body: From Dover the French coast lies roughly twenty miles away across the Strait (the 'straits' of l. 3). The light that 'Gleams and is gone' is a lighthouse on the French side, and its intermittence is the first hint of the poem's rhythm of appearance and withdrawal, picked up later in the waves that 'Begin, and cease'. The scene is set at a window looking out on the moonlit Channel, with France glimmering and England's cliffs 'Glimmering and vast': two coasts facing each other, an image of the wider European frame in which Arnold, a critic of English insularity, liked to think.

title: the addressee
short: The speaker addresses a silent companion, usually taken as the new wife; the poem is a dramatic lyric with an unheard listener.
body: The invitation turns description into dramatic address. The listener never speaks, and is named only in 'Ah, love' (l. 29); readers have generally identified her with Arnold's bride, given the honeymoon setting, though the poem itself keeps her anonymous. The silent woman has drawn later responses: Anthony Hecht's 'The Dover Bitch' (1967) gives her a cynical voice of her own and treats the speaker's gloom as a lover's self-indulgence. Note how the imperative 'Come' is immediately followed by 'Only', which qualifies the beauty just described and moves from sight to sound.

title: moon-blanch'd
short: Whitened by moonlight; the chalk shore made pale and colourless.
body: 'Blanch' means to make white or pale (French blanc). The compound describes the white chalk and shingle of the Dover shore drained of colour by moonlight, where the 'long line of spray' marks the boundary of sea and land. The pallor anticipates the poem's later emptiness: the beach that looks beautiful by moonlight becomes the 'naked shingles of the world' (l. 28). The elided spelling '-blanch'd' marks the past participle as a single syllable.

anchor: Listen! you hear the grating roar
title: the grating roar
short: The poem turns from sight to sound: the harsh scrape of shingle dragged back by retreating waves.
body: Dover's beach is of shingle (pebbles), not sand, and the undertow drags the stones seaward with a harsh rattling noise, then hurls them back up the 'high strand'. 'Grating' is both literal (the grinding of stones) and evaluative (jarring, unpleasant). The command 'Listen!' marks the poem's decisive shift from the visual calm of the opening to an auditory meditation; from here on the poem is about what is heard, and the sound becomes in turn Sophocles' 'turbid ebb and flow' and the 'melancholy, long, withdrawing roar' of faith.

title: rhythm of the waves
short: The line enacts the waves' motion with its pauses and repetition; the stanza ends on 'The eternal note of sadness'.
body: The commas break the line into short pulses that imitate the surf's alternation, and the return of 'begin' makes the line circle back on itself. 'Tremulous cadence slow', with its inverted adjective order, slows the line further. The verse paragraph has no regular stanza pattern: line lengths run from three to five stresses and rhymes recur irregularly, an organisation by sound and breath rather than by fixed form. Some critics have called the poem an early experiment towards free verse; others hear in its four irregular paragraphs the movements of a Pindaric ode.

title: The eternal note of sadness
short: The sea's sound is heard as permanent human sorrow, a note that links the speaker to Sophocles across time.
body: The 'note' is musical: the waves' cadence becomes a single sustained tone of grief. 'Eternal' matters, because the next paragraph argues that the sadness is not new; Sophocles heard it too. The sadness in this first paragraph is general and timeless, whereas the third paragraph will give the modern speaker a specific, historical cause (the retreat of faith). The poem thus moves from a universal melancholy to a particular Victorian one.

title: Sophocles
short: The Athenian tragedian (c. 496-406 BC); the passage Arnold has in mind is uncertain, with Antigone 582-92 and Trachiniae 112-21 proposed.
body: Arnold admired Sophocles as the poet who 'saw life steadily, and saw it whole' (his sonnet 'To a Friend', 1849). Many annotators point to the second stasimon of Antigone (582-92), where the chorus compares a house cursed by the gods to the sea-swell driven by Thracian winds, rolling up dark sand and beating on the headlands with a moaning roar. Some also cite Trachiniae (112-21), where Heracles' troubles are likened to waves driven over the sea by the south or north wind, as an alternative; commentators do not agree on which passage Arnold had in mind. Either way the point is the continuity of tragic perception: the same sea-sound brought misery to the Greek mind on the Aegean.

title: turbid
short: Muddy, troubled, churned up (Latin turbidus, from turba, 'disturbance').
body: 'Turbid' describes water clouded with stirred-up sediment, and figuratively a confused, disordered state. The tidal 'ebb and flow' is transferred to human misery, which recedes and returns as constantly as the tide. The word recalls the dark sand rolled up from the sea-bed in the Antigone simile. The phrase also prepares the central figure of the third paragraph, where faith too has a tide and is now at the ebb.

title: this distant northern sea
short: The English Channel contrasted with the Aegean: modern northern Europe hears the same sound as classical Greece.
body: The contrast between Greek south and modern north recurs in Arnold's criticism, which repeatedly measures Victorian England against Hellenic culture. The speaker and his companion 'Find also in the sound a thought', so the modern listener does not merely repeat Sophocles; he draws a different thought from the same sound, which the next paragraph supplies. 'Distant' implies distance in both space and time from the source of Western tragic wisdom.

title: The Sea of Faith
short: Religious belief imagined as a sea once at high tide, now ebbing; the poem's central metaphor of Victorian loss of faith.
body: Faith was 'once, too, at the full', like the tide in l. 2, encircling the world. The loss Arnold describes is cultural rather than personal conversion or apostasy: by mid-century German biblical criticism (Strauss's Life of Jesus, translated by George Eliot in 1846) and geology (Lyell's Principles, 1830-33) had made literal belief harder for educated Victorians. Arnold elsewhere hoped poetry and culture might do some of the work religion had done. The metaphor is carefully chosen: a tide that ebbs also returns, but the poem gives no sign of a coming flood, and its sound is only 'withdrawing'. Readers should note that the poem predates Darwin's Origin (1859), though its publication followed it.

title: the folds of a bright girdle furl'd
short: Faith at the full lay round the earth like a shining sash; the syntax and the sense of 'furl'd' have been debated.
body: A girdle is a belt or sash, and the image is of the sea (and faith) wrapped closely round the shore of the world, its folds bright. Commentators have puzzled over 'furl'd': a furled sail or flag is rolled up and put away, which would suggest something folded and inactive rather than spread out. Some read it simply as 'folded close', gathered and tight about the earth, giving security; others hear an ironic anticipation of the ebb. The grammar is also loose, since it is the Sea that 'Lay like the folds'. Either way, the image of an enclosing, ornamental band contrasts with the exposure of the 'naked shingles' a few lines later.

title: withdrawing roar
short: The sound of the ebbing tide becomes the sound of faith retreating; the line's length and three adjectives drag it out.
body: The 'grating roar' of l. 9 returns, now explicitly interpreted. The string of adjectives and the long vowels make the line itself feel slow and withdrawing. 'But now I only hear' insists that the speaker experiences faith only as its departure, an absence perceived as a fading sound. The 'breath / Of the night-wind' that accompanies it continues the elegiac personification.

title: shingles
short: Shingle is a beach of rounded pebbles; with the tide out, the world's edges are left bare and bleak.
body: 'Shingle' (often plural) is the loose waterworn gravel of a beach like Dover's. 'Drear' (archaic and poetic for 'dreary') and 'naked' make the receding of faith an exposure: what was clothed in the 'bright girdle' is now stripped. 'Edges' suggests the world reduced to its limits and margins. The paragraph ends on 'world', which the final paragraph immediately takes up in 'the world, which seems / To lie before us'.

anchor: Ah, love, let us be true
title: Ah, love, let us be true
short: The final turn: with public faith gone, the speaker appeals to private fidelity between lovers.
body: 'True' means faithful, constant; the word takes the place left by 'Faith'. Critics differ on how consoling this is. Some read the turn as the poem's answer, human love as the one remaining value; others note that the appeal rests on the world's lack of 'love' (l. 33), so that fidelity is a defensive alliance against a hostile world rather than a solution. The tone of the line, with its sigh 'Ah', is closer to plea than to assurance.

title: a land of dreams
short: The world 'seems' new and beautiful, as to young lovers, but the appearance is illusory.
body: The verb 'seems' sets up the contrast with 'Hath really' (l. 33). The three-part line 'So various, so beautiful, so new' gives the world's apparent promise, and may recall Adam and Eve at the close of Paradise Lost, with 'The World' 'all before them' (12.646), though the poem does not mark the echo. The 'dreams' are also the young married couple's hopes, now subjected to the poem's sober reckoning.

title: certitude
short: A list of absences: the world 'really' lacks joy, love, light, certainty, peace and relief from suffering.
body: 'Certitude' (subjective certainty, sure conviction) is the word that links the private and the intellectual crisis: the age's doubt is precisely the loss of certitude in belief. The repeated 'nor' builds a negative catalogue, the rhetorical inverse of the 'So various, so beautiful, so new' of l. 32. 'Light' recalls the light that 'Gleams and is gone' on the French coast, and prepares the 'darkling plain'.

title: darkling
short: 'Darkling' means in the dark, or growing dark; the word carries strong literary echoes from Milton and Keats.
body: 'Darkling' is an old adverb ('in the dark') also used as an adjective. Arnold's readers would hear Milton's nightingale that 'Sings darkling' (Paradise Lost 3.38-40) and Keats's 'Darkling I listen' in 'Ode to a Nightingale'. Arnold reverses those precedents: there the darkness surrounds a solitary singer, here it covers a battlefield. A. Dwight Culler treats the 'darkling plain' as Arnold's central image of the modern condition. Hardy's 'The Darkling Thrush' (1900) borrows the word, probably with Arnold in mind.

title: ignorant armies clash by night
short: Usually traced to Thucydides' account of the Athenian night attack on Epipolae at Syracuse (413 BC), where soldiers could not tell friend from foe.
body: In Thucydides 7.44 the Athenian assault on Epipolae turns to chaos in the moonlight: the troops could see shapes but could not tell whether they were friends or enemies, and some fought their own side. Arnold's father, Thomas Arnold, had edited Thucydides, and the passage is almost universally accepted as the source; other contemporary battles have also been proposed. 'Ignorant' is the key word: the combatants do not know what they fight for or against, which turns military confusion into an image of an age without certitude, its quarrels (religious, political, intellectual) conducted blindly. 'Confused alarms' (calls to arms) continues the same scene.

title: Form of the poem
short: Four verse paragraphs of unequal length, irregular line lengths and an unpredictable rhyme pattern.
body: The poem has 37 lines in paragraphs of 14, 6, 8 and 9 lines. Lines range from three to five stresses, and rhymes (night/light, stand/land/strand) recur without a scheme, so that the poem's music follows the rise and fall of the sea rather than a stanza. Critics have described it variously as proto-free verse and as a loosely Pindaric ode whose strophe and antistrophe end in catastrophe. 'Alarms' here means calls to arms (Italian all'arme).
